title: The Lady with the Lamp: The Story of Florence Nightingale
author: Grammar Stream
retoldBy: Written for Grammar Stream from the life of Florence Nightingale
blurb: The true story of Florence Nightingale, the rich girl who was told nursing was no job for a lady. Follow her to the dirty army hospital at Scutari in the Crimean War, where she carried her lantern through the wards at night, meet the brave Mary Seacole, and find out how a picture made of numbers helped to save lives.
note: A true story told for young readers. Facts and dates are drawn from standard histories, including the Florence Nightingale Museum, the National Archives, Britannica and Mary Seacole’s own Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands (1857); the war and illness are described without gory detail, and “Think about it” questions are added at the end of each chapter.

chapters.title: Chapter 1. A Girl Named After a City
paragraphs: On 12 May 1820, a baby girl was born in a grand villa in the city of Florence, in Italy. Her parents, William and Fanny Nightingale, were English, and they were travelling around Europe. They loved Florence so much that they named their new baby after it.

Florence was not the first child to be named after a city. She had a big sister, born a year earlier in Naples, and her name was Parthenope, which is the old Greek name for Naples. Everybody called her Parthe for short, and they called Florence “Flo”.

When Flo was still a baby, the family came home to England. The Nightingales were very rich. They had two large houses: Lea Hurst, in the hills of Derbyshire, where they spent the summer, and Embley Park, in Hampshire, where they spent the winter. There were servants to cook and clean, gardens to play in, and horses to ride.

Most girls in those days were taught only a little: some music, some drawing, some sewing. But Mr Nightingale taught his daughters himself, and he taught them a great deal. Florence learned Latin and Greek, French, German and Italian, history and, best of all, mathematics. She loved numbers. She liked making lists and tables, putting things in order so that she could see what they told her.

Parthe liked to stay indoors, painting and arranging flowers. Florence was different. She liked to go out with her mother to visit poor families in the villages near their homes, taking food and medicine to people who were ill. Florence would sit by a sick person’s bed and talk to them kindly. She did not mind hard work. She wanted to be useful.

When Florence was sixteen, something happened that she never forgot. She wrote that she had felt God calling her to do some special work. She did not yet know what that work would be. But she knew that her life must be about helping other people.

Her mother had other plans. Fanny Nightingale hoped that both her daughters would go to parties and balls, marry rich gentlemen, and run big houses of their own. That was what young ladies from wealthy families were supposed to do.
Florence went to the parties. She wore the beautiful dresses. But inside, she was waiting.
Think about it: Florence’s father taught her maths, which most girls did not learn. How do you think that might help her later in her life?

chapters.title: Chapter 2. Not a Job for a Lady
paragraphs: As Florence grew up, she slowly realised what her special work should be. She wanted to be a nurse.

Today, nurses are among the most trusted people in the world. But two hundred years ago it was very different. Hospitals were often dark, dirty and crowded. Most nurses had never been trained. They were poorly paid, and some of them were rough and unkind. Rich families did not go to hospital at all: doctors came to their homes. A hospital was certainly no place for a young lady.

When Florence was twenty-five, she asked her parents if she could go and learn nursing at a hospital in Salisbury, near their home. Her mother was horrified. Parthe cried and made a fuss. Even her father, who loved her very much, was upset. The answer was no.

For years, Florence felt trapped. She read everything she could find about hospitals and health. She got up early in the morning, before the rest of the house was awake, to study reports about hospitals and illnesses, filling notebooks with facts and figures.

In 1849, she went on a long journey with two kind friends, Charles and Selina Bracebridge. They sailed down the River Nile in Egypt and then went on to Greece. In Athens, near the ancient temple called the Parthenon, Florence saw some boys teasing a tiny owl that had fallen out of its nest. She rescued it at once. She named the little owl Athena, after the Greek goddess of wisdom, and from then on Athena went everywhere with her, often riding in her pocket.

On the way home in 1850, Florence visited a place she had been reading about for years. It was at Kaiserswerth, on the River Rhine in Germany, and it was run by a pastor called Theodor Fliedner and his wife. There, women called deaconesses were trained to care for the sick, as well as to look after children and teach. Everything was simple, clean and orderly, and the work was done with kindness. Florence was thrilled.
The next year, in 1851, she went back to Kaiserswerth to train for about three months. She was thirty-one years old, and at last she was learning to be a nurse.

Florence did not invent nursing. People had been caring for the sick for thousands of years, and there were already places like Kaiserswerth where nurses were trained. But Florence was about to show the whole world what good nursing could do.

In 1853, she was given her first real job: she was put in charge of a small hospital for sick ladies in Harley Street, in London. Florence was brilliant at it. She made sure there was hot water on every floor. She had bells fitted so that patients could call a nurse. She kept careful accounts of every penny. Her family still did not like it, but Florence was not going to give up now.
Think about it: Why do you think Florence’s parents did not want her to be a nurse? Do you think they were being unkind, or trying to protect her?

chapters.title: Chapter 3. A Letter About the War
paragraphs: In 1854, Britain and France joined Turkey in a war against Russia. Most of the fighting happened on a peninsula called the Crimea, beside the Black Sea, so it became known as the Crimean War.

Thousands of British soldiers sailed off to fight. Soon, terrible news came back. A newspaper reporter called William Howard Russell wrote in *The Times* that wounded and sick British soldiers were not being properly cared for. There were not enough doctors, not enough beds and not enough medicine. People in Britain were shocked and angry. Why were their soldiers being treated so badly?

Florence read the reports and knew she had to help. She wrote to a friend of hers, Sidney Herbert, who was Secretary at War, one of the ministers in charge of the army. At the very same time, Sidney Herbert was writing a letter to her! He was asking whether she would lead a group of nurses to look after the soldiers. The two letters crossed in the post.

There was no time to waste. In just a few days, Florence chose a team of thirty-eight nurses. Some were nuns, some were nurses from hospitals, and all of them had to promise to work hard and follow her instructions. Selina and Charles Bracebridge came too.
Sadly, just before she left, little Athena the owl died. Florence was heartbroken, but she could not stop to be sad for long.

On 21 October 1854, Florence and her nurses set off from London. They crossed the sea to France, took trains across the country, and sailed on from Marseille through the Mediterranean Sea. On 4 November 1854, they arrived at Scutari, in Turkey, across the water from the great city of Constantinople, which today is called Istanbul.

The British army hospital at Scutari was in a huge barracks building, so big that its long corridors seemed to go on for miles. Wounded and sick soldiers were brought there by ship from the Crimea, across the Black Sea, a long and uncomfortable journey.
When Florence walked inside, she could hardly believe her eyes.

The hospital was filthy. Men lay on the floor, some without blankets, still in the dirty clothes they had worn in battle. There were not enough bandages, plates, cups or spoons. There was no clean water to drink or to wash with. The drains under the building were blocked, and the smell was dreadful. Rats ran along the corridors, and fleas and lice were everywhere.
Worst of all, more soldiers were dying from illnesses such as cholera and typhus than from the wounds they had suffered in battle.
Florence took a deep breath, rolled up her sleeves and got ready to work.
Think about it: Florence and Sidney Herbert wrote to each other at the same time. What does that tell you about how they both felt about the soldiers?

chapters.title: Chapter 4. Scrubbing Brushes and Clean Shirts
paragraphs: You might think the army doctors would be delighted to see Florence and her nurses. But many of them were not. They did not believe that women belonged in an army hospital, and they did not like being told that things were wrong.

Florence was clever. She told her nurses not to do anything until the doctors asked them to. So for a few days, the nurses waited. They rolled bandages and sewed and sorted things out, but they did not go onto the wards.

Meanwhile, the day after they arrived, a great battle had been fought in the Crimea: the Battle of Inkerman. A few days later, ships full of wounded men began to arrive. There were far too many patients for the doctors to manage alone, and at last they asked the nurses for help.

Florence was ready. She was a brilliant organiser. She had brought supplies with her, and she had money collected by kind people in Britain, so she bought what the hospital needed: shirts, socks, sheets, soap, scrubbing brushes, knives and forks, and much more. She set up kitchens to cook proper food for the patients who were too ill to eat the army’s tough meat. She arranged for clothes and bedding to be properly washed. The nurses scrubbed the floors and walls until they were clean.
Florence worked for hours and hours every day. She looked after patients herself, wrote letters, gave orders, and kept careful records of everything.

But even with all their hard work, that first winter was terrible. Many soldiers still died, and the number of deaths actually rose. Something else was wrong, something that scrubbing brushes could not fix.

In March 1855, a team of experts sent by the government arrived at Scutari. It was called the Sanitary Commission, and its job was to make the hospital a healthier place. They found that the drains under the building were blocked and leaking. The air inside was stale and did not move. The water supply was dirty.

The Sanitary Commission set to work. Workers flushed out and repaired the drains, cleaned up the water and let fresh air flow through the wards. Within a few weeks, the number of soldiers dying fell sharply.

Florence watched and learned. She now understood that dirt, bad drains and stale air could be just as deadly as any battle. It was a lesson she would spend the rest of her life teaching to everybody who would listen.
Think about it: Why do you think the number of deaths went down so quickly after the drains were mended and fresh air came in?

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Lady with the Lamp
paragraphs: When night came at Scutari, the doctors went to bed, and the long corridors grew dark and quiet. But Florence did not go to bed. Night after night, she walked through the wards, checking on the sick and wounded men.

She carried a lantern to light her way. It was a Turkish lantern. Its shade was made of pleated cloth stretched between two metal ends, so that it could fold up flat, and a candle burned inside it. In many pictures, Florence is shown holding a little oil lamp, shaped a bit like a genie’s lamp. But that was the artists’ idea. The lamp she really carried was a folding lantern, and one that is believed to be hers is kept today in the Florence Nightingale Museum in London.

As she walked, she stopped by the beds. She spoke gently to the men who could not sleep. She made sure that the very sick were comfortable. To the soldiers, many of them far from home and frightened, the soft glow of her lantern coming down the corridor was a comfort.

A newspaper report sent home from Scutari described her walking alone with a little lamp in her hand, making her rounds when everyone else had gone to sleep. Soon everybody in Britain was talking about her. They called her “the Lady with the Lamp”.

Florence also cared about the soldiers in other ways. She wrote letters home for men who were too ill to write, or who had never learned how. She set up reading rooms, so that soldiers who were getting better had something to do. She helped them send their wages home to their families. People back then often thought that ordinary soldiers did not deserve much care. Florence believed that every one of them mattered.

Back in Britain, Florence became a heroine. People bought pictures of her and sang songs about her. Queen Victoria sent her a beautiful brooch, designed by Prince Albert, with the words “Blessed are the merciful” on it.

Florence did not care about being famous. She cared about the work. In the spring of 1855, she sailed across the Black Sea to visit the hospitals in the Crimea itself. There she caught a terrible fever and became dangerously ill. For a while, people feared she might die. Slowly she got better, and she went back to work, but she would never be really strong and well again.
Think about it: Why do you think the soldiers were so glad to see Florence’s lantern in the middle of the night?

chapters.title: Chapter 6. Mother Seacole
paragraphs: Florence was not the only woman who travelled a long way to help the soldiers in the Crimean War. Another woman, called Mary Seacole, had a remarkable story too.

Mary was born in 1805 in Kingston, on the island of Jamaica, in the Caribbean. Her father was a Scottish soldier. Her mother was a healer, who looked after sick people in the boarding house she ran, using medicines made from plants and herbs. Mary watched her mother and learned everything she could. Even as a little girl, she pretended to look after her doll when it was “ill”.
When Mary grew up, she travelled to many places. She helped to nurse people with deadly diseases such as cholera and yellow fever, and she became very good at it.

When she heard about the war, Mary decided that she wanted to help the soldiers. Some of them were men she had known in Jamaica. In 1854 she travelled to London and asked to join the nurses who were going to the war. But she was turned down. She was disappointed, but she did not give up.

Mary decided to go anyway, and to pay for the journey herself. She went into business with a man called Thomas Day, and in 1855 they opened a place they called the British Hotel, near Balaclava in the Crimea. It was not really a hotel, more a shop and a canteen. Mary sold warm meals, drinks and all kinds of supplies to the officers. She also gave medicines and care to soldiers who were sick and wounded, and she sometimes went out close to the battlefields, with her bag of bandages and medicines, to look after injured men.
The soldiers loved her. They called her “Mother Seacole”.

On her way to the Crimea, Mary stopped at Scutari and met Florence Nightingale. Florence was busy with her own huge hospital, and the two women did not work together. Each of them helped the soldiers in her own way: Florence by organising a great hospital and changing how hospitals were run, and Mary by her own brave and kind work near the fighting.

After the war, Mary wrote a book about her life called *Wonderful Adventures of Mrs Seacole in Many Lands*. It came out in 1857. For many years she was forgotten, but today she is remembered and honoured. In 2016, a statue of Mary Seacole was put up in the garden of St Thomas’ Hospital in London.
Think about it: Mary was turned down, but she went anyway. What does that tell you about the kind of person she was?

chapters.title: Chapter 7. A Picture That Saved Lives
paragraphs: In March 1856, the Crimean War came to an end. Florence stayed until the very last soldiers had left the hospitals. Then, in the summer of 1856, she came home.

The whole country wanted to welcome her with bands and cheering crowds. But Florence did not want any fuss. She travelled quietly, without telling anybody, and in August 1856 she arrived back at Lea Hurst, in Derbyshire. It is said that she walked up to the house from the railway station on her own, and nobody recognised her.

Florence was famous now, but she was not happy. She could not stop thinking about all the soldiers who had died, not in battle, but from diseases that could have been prevented. She was determined that it must never happen again.

Soon after she came home, Queen Victoria invited Florence to visit her at Balmoral Castle, in Scotland. Florence told the Queen and Prince Albert what she had seen. She wanted the army to change the way it looked after its soldiers.
But Florence knew that just telling people was not enough. She needed proof. So she went back to the thing she had loved since she was a little girl: numbers.

Working with a clever statistician called William Farr, Florence studied the records of how many soldiers had died during the war, and why. A statistician is someone who collects numbers and works out what they show. The figures told a shocking story. Far more soldiers had died from illnesses caused by dirt, bad drains and stale air than had died from their wounds.
Florence knew that a long list of numbers can be hard to understand, especially for busy people. So she turned the numbers into a picture.

Her picture looked a bit like a flower, so it is often called a rose diagram. It is a circle cut into twelve wedges, like slices of a cake, one slice for each month of the year. The bigger the slice, the more soldiers died that month. Each slice was coloured in. The blue part showed soldiers who died of diseases that could have been prevented. The red part showed soldiers who died of wounds. The black part showed other causes. Florence drew two of these circles side by side, one for each year of the war.

When people looked at the rose, they saw at once that the blue parts were enormous, much bigger than the red parts. They could also see how much smaller the slices became after the hospitals were cleaned up. You did not need to be good at maths to understand it.

Florence’s work helped to persuade the government to make army hospitals and barracks cleaner and healthier. In 1858, she became the first woman to be made a member of the Royal Statistical Society, a group of experts in numbers.

Florence was often ill after the war. She spent much of the rest of her life working from her room at home in London, sometimes from her bed. But she never stopped working. She wrote thousands of letters and met important visitors who came to ask her advice.
Think about it: Why do you think a picture was better than a long list of numbers for showing people what had gone wrong?

chapters.title: Chapter 8. Nurses for the Whole World
paragraphs: While Florence was away at the war, people in Britain had given money to say thank you for her work. They gave so much that it became a huge sum, called the Nightingale Fund. Florence decided to use it to do something she had dreamed of for years: to train nurses properly.

In 1860, the Nightingale Training School for nurses opened at St Thomas’ Hospital, in London. The first group of fifteen young women came to learn. They studied for a year, living together in a home at the hospital, and they learned how to care for patients carefully, cleanly and kindly. When they had finished, many of them went on to train other nurses, in Britain and in other countries. Slowly, nursing became a skilled and respected job.

A little earlier, in 1859, Florence had written a book called *Notes on Nursing*. It was not only for nurses in hospitals. It was written for anyone who had to look after somebody who was ill, at home. In it, Florence wrote about the things that help sick people get better: fresh air, light, warmth, quiet, clean rooms and good food. She also wrote that a nurse ought to wash her hands very often during the day. Today, we know just how important that is.
Florence lived to be a very old lady. In 1907, King Edward VII gave her the Order of Merit, a very special honour. She was the first woman ever to receive it.

Florence Nightingale died peacefully in her sleep on 13 August 1910, at her home in London. She was ninety years old. Her family were offered a grave for her in Westminster Abbey, where kings and queens are buried, but Florence had asked for something simpler. She was buried in the churchyard of St Margaret’s Church at East Wellow, near her old home at Embley, in Hampshire.

Florence did not invent nursing, and she did not do everything on her own. But she showed the world that nurses need proper training, that clean hospitals save lives, and that numbers can be used to make people listen.

Every year, on 12 May, Florence’s birthday, nurses all over the world celebrate International Nurses Day. And whenever a nurse checks on a patient in the middle of the night, by the soft light of a lamp, you can think of the Lady with the Lamp, walking down that long dark corridor at Scutari.
Think about it: Florence was a nurse, a writer and a mathematician. Which of the things she did do you think was the most important, and why?
